title: How Sushi Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and preparation of sushi. They cover its folklore origins in Southeast Asia (fermented fish packed in rice), the Japanese shift to adding sake and then rice vinegar, the Osaka-style oshi sushi and Yohei Hanaya's hand-formed nigiri in Edo, and the spread of sushi to America through the California roll and Los Angeles restaurants. They discuss sushi fish and toppings (sashimi-grade and frozen fish, tuna varieties, freshwater eel, tamago, roe, avocado), etiquette (eating nigiri with hands, sparing soy sauce, wasabi, sake pouring), sushi chef training, and a step-by-step guide to making sushi rice, nigiri, maki, and hand rolls. The episode closes with listener mail about rotation plasty.

segments.title: Opening banter and sushi misconceptions
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about sushi appetite and clarify that sushi refers to vinegared rice, not raw fish (sashimi). They note raw fish served in US must be frozen by law except tuna, and that sushi is a genre of food.

segments.title: Early origins of sushi
segments.summary: Folklore about an old woman and osprey nests is discussed and dismissed. The earliest sushi was fish fermented in cooked rice in Southeast Asia, which preserved the fish; the rice was discarded. Later in Japan, the fish was gutted, soaked in sake, and packed with rice, shortening the process from about a year and a half.

segments.title: Rise of vinegar rice, oshi sushi and nigiri
segments.summary: Tokugawa Ieyasu moved the capital to Edo (later Tokyo). Rice vinegar sped preparation. Osaka-style oshi sushi was pressed in boxes. Yohei Hanaya in Edo in the 1820s made hand-formed nigiri at a street cart, which the hosts credit as the origin of modern sushi. After the Great Kanto earthquake, sushi moved into restaurants.

segments.title: Sushi's spread to America and New York
segments.summary: Sushi booms in Japan after refrigeration and the postwar economy. It was adopted in Los Angeles in the 1960s at Kawafuku. Restaurants like Osho in Hollywood followed in 1970. Hosts describe Nobu in New York and the California roll, created in 1973, as a gateway for Americans.

segments.title: Vegetables, toppings and fish selection
segments.summary: Discussion of vegetable sushi fillings like asparagus, cucumber and mushrooms, and cauliflower. They explain that saltwater fish are preferred over freshwater fish because of parasites, though freshwater eel is popular and is typically cooked. Fish choice includes yellowtail, hamachi and salmon.

segments.title: Bluefin tuna and live sushi
segments.summary: Bluefin tuna is the most prized, with the Japanese prizing it only from the 1950s. A 490-pound bluefin sold at the Tokyo fish market for about 1.8 million dollars. Ikizukuri live sushi, including a live frog and a squid scene in Oldboy, is discussed along with ethical concerns about tuna farming.

segments.title: Roe, tamago, avocado and sushi toppings
segments.summary: Hosts describe roe (ikura and smelt roe), tamago as a sweet cooked egg omelet, avocado as a common addition, and unusual toppings like fried chicken and cereal that they dismiss.

segments.title: Sushi etiquette, soy sauce, wasabi and sake
segments.summary: Guidance on eating nigiri with fingers, dipping fish side only, sparing soy sauce, and not drowning rice. Real wasabi is rare in the US; most is horseradish and mustard dyed green. Sake is traditionally poured for others, and women chefs face discrimination in Japan. Sushi chefs train for years.

segments.title: How to make sushi at home
segments.summary: Step-by-step guide to buying sashimi-grade fish, washing and cooking sushi rice, seasoning with rice vinegar, sugar and salt, and rolling nigiri, oshi, futomaki, uramaki and hand rolls. Hosts also mention a wooden rice paddle and bamboo mat.

segments.title: Listener mail: rotation plasty
segments.summary: Listener Kelly writes about rotation plasty, a limb-salvage procedure where the lower leg is reattached backward so the ankle functions as a knee.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts point listeners to HowStuffWorks search and social channels and sign off.
